frozen-set-read-mostly.title: Use FrozenSet<T> for read-mostly sets
frozen-set-read-mostly.short: Freeze an immutable-after-build set for efficient lookups.
frozen-set-read-mostly.summary: FrozenSet<T> optimizes a set that will not change after construction for read operations such as Contains. It fits configuration values and known command sets.
frozen-set-read-mostly.why: It pays construction cost up front so repeated lookups can be optimized afterward.
frozen-set-read-mostly.tips: Use HashSet<T> when elements change frequently, and choose FrozenSet<T> where enough reads justify freezing.

system-threading-lock.title: Synchronize with System.Threading.Lock
system-threading-lock.short: Use the dedicated Lock type as a lock statement target.
system-threading-lock.summary: System.Threading.Lock is a dedicated synchronization primitive that works with the lock statement to protect shared state from concurrent access.
system-threading-lock.why: A synchronization-specific type makes intent clearer than locking on an arbitrary object.
system-threading-lock.tips: Keep critical sections short and do not await while holding the lock.

pipereader-consume-buffer.title: Advance PipeReader after consuming a buffer
pipereader-consume-buffer.summary: After processing the buffer returned by PipeReader.ReadAsync, call AdvanceTo to report what was consumed and examined.
pipereader-consume-buffer.why: Without advancement, PipeReader cannot know which buffered data may be reused or released.
pipereader-consume-buffer.tips: When only part of a buffer is processed, distinguish consumed from examined and follow the PipeReader read contract carefully.

json-source-generation.title: Use System.Text.Json source generation
json-source-generation.short: Generate JSON type metadata at build time.
json-source-generation.summary: JsonSerializerContext and JsonSerializable can generate serialization metadata for known types during the build.
json-source-generation.why: This can reduce runtime reflection and startup work and works well with AOT scenarios.
json-source-generation.tips: Register every required type and keep naming and serializer options consistent with the generated context.

memorycache-size-limit.title: Set entry Size when using MemoryCache SizeLimit
memorycache-size-limit.short: Give entries a size in a size-limited cache.
memorycache-size-limit.summary: When a MemoryCache is configured with MemoryCacheOptions.SizeLimit, entries need a Size measured in the same application-defined units.
memorycache-size-limit.why: MemoryCache does not measure the actual memory footprint of arbitrary objects; the application defines the sizing unit.
memorycache-size-limit.tips: Use a dedicated sizing policy and consistent units rather than adding Size mechanically to an unrestricted shared cache.

enumerable-chunk-batching.title: Batch sequences with Enumerable.Chunk
enumerable-chunk-batching.short: Split enumeration into arrays of a maximum size.
enumerable-chunk-batching.summary: Chunk divides an IEnumerable<T> in order into arrays containing up to the requested number of elements. It is useful for batched API calls and writes.
enumerable-chunk-batching.why: It makes batch boundaries explicit without manually maintaining a counter and temporary list.
enumerable-chunk-batching.tips: Each chunk is allocated as an array, so consider alternatives if allocations matter for very large streams.

parallel-foreachasync.title: Control concurrency with Parallel.ForEachAsync
parallel-foreachasync.short: Process many items concurrently with a limit.
parallel-foreachasync.summary: Parallel.ForEachAsync runs an asynchronous delegate over sequence elements and accepts ParallelOptions for cancellation and maximum parallelism.
parallel-foreachasync.why: A concurrency limit is easier to control than creating an unbounded number of tasks against a service or CPU.
parallel-foreachasync.tips: Choose parallelism from measurements and external service limits rather than using one fixed value everywhere.

objectpool-reuse.title: Reuse hot-path objects with ObjectPool<T>
objectpool-reuse.short: Borrow and return temporary objects that are expensive to recreate.
objectpool-reuse.summary: ObjectPool<T> can reuse temporary objects to reduce allocations on hot paths.
objectpool-reuse.why: Repeated construction of larger temporary buffers or StringBuilder instances can create avoidable GC pressure.
objectpool-reuse.tips: Design pooled objects so their state can be reset, return them in finally, and introduce pooling only after measuring a need.

channel-trywrite-backpressure.title: Do not ignore a failed Channel.TryWrite
channel-trywrite-backpressure.short: Handle a full bounded channel explicitly.
channel-trywrite-backpressure.summary: TryWrite attempts a non-waiting channel write and returns false when it cannot write immediately. Ignoring that result can silently lose an item.
channel-trywrite-backpressure.why: A bounded channel being full is a normal reason for TryWrite to fail.
channel-trywrite-backpressure.tips: When loss is not allowed, define a backpressure policy such as falling back to WriteAsync when TryWrite returns false.

stringbuilder-clear-reuse.title: Reuse StringBuilder capacity with Clear
stringbuilder-clear-reuse.short: Clear content while retaining a builder for another construction.
stringbuilder-clear-reuse.summary: StringBuilder.Clear resets Length to zero so the same instance can be used for the next string construction.
stringbuilder-clear-reuse.why: In a tight loop, reusing existing capacity can avoid repeatedly creating builders.
stringbuilder-clear-reuse.tips: A builder that once held a huge string may retain substantial capacity, so long-lived reuse is not automatically better; measure it.
